planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart. Fruiting occurs on second-year canes, typically May-June in zones 7-9.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5); Cherokee is one of the earliest University of Arkansas thornless blackberry releases, introduced in the early 1970s and long a standard against which newer thornless varieties are measured. Canes are erect and self-supporting, requiring only light trellising, and produce medium-to-large, firm, well-flavored black berries in a concentrated early-to-mid season harvest. Because it is an older release, Cherokee is generally less productive and somewhat more disease-prone than modern Arkansas thornless cultivars like Natchez or Ouachita, but its cold hardiness and long track record still make it a dependable choice. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 per plant to keep the planting productive.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Fruit Breeding — Blackberry Cultivar History
North Carolina State University Extension — Blackberry Cultivars

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; unlike most blackberries, Prime-Ark Freedom fruits on first-year primocanes in late summer to fall as well as on second-year floricanes the following early summer, giving two harvest windows.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun; Prime-Ark Freedom is a University of Arkansas thornless primocane-fruiting blackberry, the first thornless release in the Prime-Ark series, notable for producing a fall crop on current-season canes in addition to the traditional early-summer crop on overwintered canes. Berries are large, firm, and glossy black with good flavor. For a single, larger fall crop, mow or cut all canes to the ground in winter and let only primocanes fruit that year; for two crops, leave some canes standing to fruit as floricanes in early summer while new primocanes develop for a fall crop. This flexibility makes it a popular choice for extending the blackberry season well into fall in the Gulf South.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Fruit Breeding — Prime-Ark Freedom release notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Blackberry Variety Trials

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart. Caddo is a compact, erect, thornless blackberry that fruits in the second year and needs only minimal trellising due to its shorter, sturdy canes.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun; Caddo is a more recent University of Arkansas thornless blackberry release, bred for a compact, upright plant habit that is noticeably shorter and tidier than older erect thornless cultivars, making it well suited to smaller home gardens and even large containers. It ripens early in the season, ahead of many other thornless varieties, with large, firm, glossy black, well-flavored berries. The compact habit reduces the need for trellising and makes hand harvest easier. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest few per plant to maintain good air circulation and fruit size.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Fruit Breeding — Caddo release notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Blackberry Variety Trials

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart, and provide a two-wire trellis for the vigorous, thorny canes.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun and trellis the vigorous, thorny canes for support and easier harvest. Chickasaw is an older University of Arkansas blackberry release valued for its very large fruit size and vigorous, productive canes, ripening in the early-to-mid part of the season. Unlike the newer thornless Arkansas releases, Chickasaw retains thorns, so plant it where hand-picking around thorny canes is acceptable in exchange for its exceptionally large, firm, flavorful berries. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 canes per plant to sustain vigor and berry size in subsequent years.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Fruit Breeding — Blackberry Cultivar History
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Blackberry Variety Trials

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained, organically rich soil; Southland has an unusually low chill requirement for a red raspberry, allowing it to break dormancy and fruit reliably in mild southern winters where most red raspberries fail to set a crop.

directions: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest parts of zone 9, and mulch well to keep roots cool. Southland is one of the few red raspberry cultivars bred specifically for adaptation to mild southern winters, with a low chilling-hour requirement that lets it flower and fruit where standard northern raspberries decline within a season or two from insufficient winter chill. It produces a light-to-moderate crop of medium-sized, sweet-tart red berries in late spring, with some plants also producing a smaller fall crop on primocanes. Yields are modest compared with northern raspberry cultivars grown in their ideal climate, but Southland remains one of the more dependable options for gardeners in zone 8-9 who want to try growing red raspberries. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to maintain airflow and reduce disease in humid conditions.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Raspberry Cultivars for the South
University of Georgia Extension — Bramble Fruits for the Home Garden
